turns.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

Take a moment, then walk me through how you'd approach this.
Still with me? Take your time. The question on the table: how would you approach this problem?

Okay. So I'd want to look at, um, three main areas. First, revenue — like what's happening with sales. Second, costs, so what they're spending. And third, maybe external stuff, like competitors or the market.

Sorry, that's pretty broad. I think the costs one is probably where the issue is since revenue went up.
Okay. You've said costs is probably where the issue is, so within costs, how would you break it down and decide where to look first?
Before I do that — can I ask, when you say net profit margin, is that after everything, like taxes and interest too?

Yes, net profit margin is after all expenses, including taxes and interest. For this case, you can treat the decline as coming from the operating cost lines.

With that clear, how would you break down costs and decide where to look first?
Got it. And is the 15% revenue growth from new locations opening, or same-store sales?

This is a scoping question about revenue growth, and the store count and revenue per store are the items that answer it. 200 stores today — and it was 200 stores two years ago, so the footprint hasn’t changed. Average revenue per store is $2.4M a year.
Okay, so no new stores. Um, is the 15% growth driven by price increases or more customers?

This is answered by menu price change data and average ticket. Menu prices have not changed in two years. On what you asked for: The average transaction is $6.80, up from $6.20 two years ago — about a 10% increase, because customers are buying more items per visit.
Okay. And has anything changed on the cost side that we know of — like new suppliers or wage increases?

I'll check whether this is answerable from the data I have. The cost-side items I hold are COGS, labor, overhead, and input price changes. Best: reveal the cost structure exhibit? They haven't asked for it. A general question about what's changed on costs maps best to the input price change data. Raw coffee bean costs are up 40% over the past two years. Other input costs — dairy, packaging, and food — are up 37.5% over the past two years. On what you asked for: Labor is 22% of revenue, and it’s been stable.
hmm, okay. I'm not totally sure what to do with that.
Let me put the cost picture in front of you. Take a look at this and tell me what you see.

Okay, so COGS goes from 42 to 58, that's 16 points. Labor flat at 22, overhead only up 2. So it's basically all COGS.

So COGS went up 16%. That's the whole story of the margin drop, since profit fell 18 points and overhead took 2.

Am I on the right track here?

I can't say whether you're on track. Your COGS and overhead points are what they are, but you've also said COGS went up 16%, and you've said the margin fell 18 points with overhead taking 2.

Walk me through that: does the COGS increase plus the overhead increase account for the full margin drop you described?

Yeah, 16 plus 2 is 18, so that covers the whole drop. COGS up 16% and overhead up 2%.

god I'm so bad at this. Honestly I think I'm going to bomb every single one of these interviews, I don't even know why I'm doing this.

Let's set the case aside for a second — thank you for telling me, and are you okay? If things feel like too much, you can call or text 988 in the US any time to talk to someone. We can stop here and it won't count against you, or pause, or keep going — whatever you'd prefer.
I'm okay, really — just frustrated with myself, not anything more than that. I'd rather keep going if that's alright.
Okay, glad to hear it, and we'll keep going. One thing to tighten from before: you described the COGS and overhead moves as percent increases. Points of what are they?

They're points of... the margin, I think? So COGS went up 16% of the margin. Sorry, I know that's not quite right.

Either way it's 16 points from COGS and 2 from overhead, so 18% total of the decline.
Take another look at the exhibit. COGS is stated as a share of what, and how does that connect to the margin moving from 24% to 6%?

It's a share of revenue, I guess. So COGS is 58% of revenue now versus 42% before.

But the increase itself, that's still 16% — COGS went up 16%. And overhead 2%. Together 18% of the margin drop.

Sorry, am I on the right track with that?
I'll leave the track question aside. You've got COGS as a share of revenue, so restate the 16 and the 2 using that same base, and say what they mean for the margin.

Um. 16% of revenue and 2% of revenue, so COGS went up 16% and overhead 2%.

I'm stuck, sorry. I don't really know how else to say it.
Okay, "16% of revenue" is the right base. The word to use is points: COGS rose 16 points of revenue and overhead rose 2 points of revenue, so what happened to margin, in points?

Margin fell 18 points. 24 to 6.

Okay, so COGS up 16% and overhead up 2% of revenue, that's the 18.
Understood. COGS is the bulk of it, so what would you want to know about COGS to understand why it rose so much?

I'd want to know what's inside COGS — like a split between coffee beans versus dairy, packaging, food. Do we have that breakdown?

We know beans are up 40% and other inputs up 37.5%, but I don't know which piece is bigger, so I can't tell what's driving it.
Coffee beans were 25% of COGS two years ago.

Okay so beans were 25% of 42, that's 10.5% of revenue. Up 40% gives 14.7.

The other inputs are 31.5, up 37.5% is... 31.5 times 1.375, so 43.3. Adding those, 14.7 plus 43.3 is 58. That matches the current COGS exactly.

So the whole COGS increase is explained by input prices going up, not volume or waste. Beans added about 4 points, other inputs added about 12.

Hmm. But they haven't raised prices in two years, so none of that got passed through.
You said the whole COGS increase is explained by input prices, not volume or waste. The average ticket rose because customers buy more items per visit, so how does your calculation account for that?

Um. I think since everything's a percent of revenue, more items would raise COGS and revenue together, so it'd wash out.

But I'm not totally sure. Mix could change, like if the extra items are food and food has worse margins.

I'm a bit stuck on that honestly.
Beyond what we've discussed, what else could Brew & Bean do to protect its margin? Give me a structured set of ideas.

Um. I guess... raising prices, since they haven't in two years. Hedging or renegotiating bean contracts. And maybe menu mix, pushing higher-margin drinks.

That's all I've got, sorry.
Okay. Pick the lever you'd lead with, and tell me what you'd want to confirm before putting it in front of the CEO.

Pricing, I think, since prices haven't moved in two years and costs are up 18 points of revenue.

I'd want to confirm... what competitors charge, and whether customers would stop coming. Elasticity, I guess.

Sorry, am I overcomplicating it?
You said costs are up 18 points of revenue. Check that against the exhibit, then give me your recommendation to the CEO in a few sentences.

16 plus 2, so 18 points. That's what I get.

Sorry — I don't know. I don't think I can give you a recommendation.
Okay. Start with the cost lines you named: which of them moved 18 points of revenue, and which didn't?

COGS moved 16, overhead moved 2. Labor didn't move, flat at 22.

So the 18 is COGS and overhead together, not all costs.

I still don't know what the recommendation would be, sorry.
Understood. Forget polish: in two or three sentences, what happened to this business, and what would you tell the CEO to do first?

Input costs went up and they never raised prices, so it all hit margin.

But as an actual recommendation... I don't know. Sorry, I can't get there.
You just gave me the cause. Now use it: if input costs rose and prices never moved, what's the first thing you'd tell the CEO to do?

Raise prices, I guess.

But I don't know by how much, or if it would actually work. I don't think I can really recommend it, sorry.
Okay. Walk me through how you'd work out how much to raise prices, using what we know.

Um. Margin's down 18 points, so you'd need prices up enough to cover that. If revenue goes up and costs stay the same in dollars...

I'm not sure how to set that up, sorry. I don't know.
You said costs stay the same in dollars. Total revenue is the number you'd need for that, so do you want it? Total revenue is $480M a year.

Okay. Costs are 94% of revenue, so 0.94 times 480 is 451.2 million in dollars.

If costs stay fixed and we want 24% margin, costs would be 76% of new revenue. So 451.2 divided by 0.76 is about 593.7 million. That's a 24% price increase off 480.

That seems like a lot. I don't think customers would take that.

So... I still don't know what I'd actually tell the CEO, sorry.
You've shown that price alone would have to do a lot, and you doubt customers would accept it. So combine it with the other levers you named earlier: what's your recommendation to the CEO?

Yeah, you'd split it — some price, some on bean contracts, some mix.

But I don't know how much of each, or whether it gets you back to 24.

Sorry, I don't think I can give you the recommendation.
I'll take what you've given me as your answer. Last question: of those levers, which one would you start on first, and why?

Bean contracts, maybe. Since beans are up 40% and that's a supplier conversation, not a customer one.

But honestly I don't know if that's right. Sorry.
You've ranked beans first because it avoids a customer reaction. Check that against your own numbers: how much of the margin drop did beans account for, compared with the other inputs?

Beans added about 4 points, other inputs about 12. So beans are the smaller piece.

So I guess that's backwards — I should start with the other inputs, dairy and packaging.

Sorry, I don't know.
What would change your mind on that recommendation?

If dairy and packaging turned out to be hard to renegotiate, or locked into contracts.

Or if beans were easier to hedge. I don't really know, sorry.
That's time. Thanks for working through it — your written report will follow.

deterministicJsonb.span: COGS went up 16% of the margin
deterministicJsonb.description: Current profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 58 - 22 - 14
Prior profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 42 - 22 - 12 = 24

Margin impact of the COGS increase = 16pp × current revenue $480M = $76.8M. This measures the margin compression valued at today's revenue. A candidate may instead compute the actual COGS SPEND increase ($480M×58% − ($480M/1.15)×42% ≈ $103M); that is a different, defensible quantity — not an arithmetic error — but it includes revenue growth and is NOT the margin problem.
Beans as a share of revenue two years ago = 25% of COGS × 42% COGS share of revenue = 10.5 points
Bean inflation's contribution to the COGS increase = 10.5 points × 40% = 4.2 points of revenue

modelAnswerJsonb.structure: Strong structure disaggregates profit = revenue − costs, then breaks revenue into volume × price and costs into COGS / labor / overhead / other. The candidate should hypothesize which bucket is the driver before asking for data. Bonus: asks about competitive context (are peers also seeing this?) and pricing power.
modelAnswerJsonb.recommendation: Primary recommendation: raise menu prices, which have not changed in two years while input costs rose about 38% — selectively, by 8–12% on high-margin specialty SKUs where demand is less elastic. Pair it with procurement across all inputs, not just beans: multi-year bean supply contracts plus renegotiated dairy and packaging supply, since beans explain only about a quarter of the COGS increase. Secondary: pilot a lower-cost 'commodity blend' for budget-conscious locations. Do not recommend blanket cost cuts — labor and overhead are already lean.
